content: 1. In mineralogy, diamond is an allotrope of carbon where the carbon atoms are arranged in an isometric-hexoctahedral crystal lattice. 2. Diamonds are renowned for their exceptional hardness and high dispersion of light, making them valuable for industrial applications and jewelry. 3. Diamond is the hardest naturally occurring mineral known. 4. 5. Currently, aggregated diamond nanorods, created using ultrahard fullerite (C60), are confirmed to be harder than diamonds, though other materials like cubic boron nitride, rhenium diboride, and ultrahard fullerite itself are comparable. 6. Diamonds are celebrated for their superlative physical properties, including their ability to serve as excellent abrasives, as they can only be scratched by other diamonds or similarly hard materials like borazon or ultrahard fullerite. 7. Approximately 130 million carats (26,000 kg) of diamonds are mined annually, with a total value of nearly USD $9 billion, and about 100,000 kg (220,000 lb) are synthesized each year. 8. The name diamond originates from the ancient Greek word adamas, meaning invincible or untamed, derived from a(un-) and damao (to overpower or tame). 9. 10. The popularity of diamonds has increased since the 19th century due to improved supply, advancements in cutting and polishing techniques, global economic growth, and innovative advertising campaigns. 11. Diamonds are commonly evaluated based on the Four Cs: carat, clarity, color, and cut. 12. Roughly 49% of diamonds originate from central and southern Africa, though significant sources have also been discovered in Canada, India, Russia, Brazil, and Australia. 13. Diamonds are mined from kimberlite and lamproite volcanic pipes, which transport diamond crystals formed deep within the Earth to the surface. 14. The mining and distribution of natural diamonds are often controversial, particularly concerning the sale of conflict diamonds (also known as blood diamonds) by African paramilitary groups. 15. A diamond is a transparent crystal composed of tetrahedrally bonded carbon atoms, crystallizing into a face-centered cubic diamond lattice structure. 16. Diamonds are utilized in various applications due to their exceptional physical characteristics, including extreme hardness, high dispersion index, and extremely high thermal conductivity (900–2320 W/m·K). 17. At temperatures above 1700°C (1973 K / 3583°F), diamond converts to graphite. 18. Naturally occurring diamonds have a density ranging from 3.15 to 3.53 g/cm³, with very pure diamonds typically close to 3.52 g/cm³. 19. Diamond is the hardest natural material known, with a hardness of 10 (the highest) on the Mohs scale of mineral hardness. 20. The hardest diamonds in the world are found in the New England area of New South Wales, Australia, and are used to polish other diamonds. 21. The hardness of diamonds is influenced by their crystal growth form, with single-stage growth crystals being harder than those with multiple growth stages, which may contain inclusions, flaws, and defect planes. 22. Diamond's hardness contributes to its suitability as a gemstone, as it maintains its polish extremely well and resists scratching, making it ideal for daily wear, such as in engagement or wedding rings. 23. Industrial use of diamonds has historically been associated with their hardness, making them ideal for cutting and grinding tools. 24. As the hardest known natural material, diamond can polish, cut, or wear away any material, including other diamonds. 25. However, diamond is not suitable for machining ferrous alloys at high speeds due to carbon's solubility in iron at high temperatures, which increases wear on diamond tools. 26. Common industrial applications include diamond-tipped drill bits and saws, as well as diamond powder used as an abrasive. 27. Industrial-grade diamonds, which are unsuitable for use as gems or synthetically produced, are economically feasible for industrial applications. 28. Some blue diamonds are natural semiconductors, while most other diamonds are excellent electrical insulators. 29. Substantial electrical conductivity has been observed in undoped diamonds when exposed to air. 30.4 MN·m−3/2, is good compared to other gemstones but poor compared to most engineering materials. 31. Diamond is more fragile in certain orientations due to its macroscopic geometry. 32. Diamond color can range from blue, green, black, translucent white, pink, violet, orange, purple, and red, with yellow and brown being the most common. 33. Black diamonds are not truly black but contain numerous dark inclusions that give them their dark appearance. 34. Colored diamonds contain impurities or structural defects that cause their coloration, while pure or nearly pure diamonds are transparent and colorless. 35. The most common impurity in diamonds is nitrogen, which causes yellow coloration depending on its type and concentration. 36. The Gemological Institute of America (GIA) classifies low-saturation yellow and brown diamonds as within the normal color range, grading them from D (colorless) to Z (light yellow). 37. In October 2007, a blue diamond fetched nearly $8 million, with its blue hue resulting from trace amounts of boron in its crystal structure. 38. Diamonds can be identified by their high thermal conductivity and high refractive index, though other materials may have similar refractivity. 39. Diamonds can cut glass, but other materials above glass on the Mohs scale, such as quartz, can also do so. 40. Diamonds easily scratch other diamonds, but this damages both diamonds. 41. 42. These conditions are met in the lithospheric mantle beneath stable continental plates and at meteorite impact sites. 43. Diamonds formed in cratons occur at depths of 140–190 kilometers (90–120 miles), though occasionally at depths of 300–400 km (180–250 miles). 44. 45. Long residence in the cratonic lithosphere allows diamond crystals to grow larger. 46. Carbon isotope studies reveal that the carbon in diamonds originates from both inorganic and organic sources. 47. Harzburgitic diamonds form from inorganic carbon deep in the Earth's mantle, while eclogitic diamonds contain organic carbon from surface detritus subducted into the mantle. 48. Diamonds that have reached the Earth's surface are generally very old, ranging from under 1 billion to 3.3 billion years old. 49. Diamonds often occur as euhedral or rounded octahedra and twinned octahedra known as macles. 50. Diamond crystals can have rounded edges and may form double twinned crystals. 51. Diamonds are sometimes coated in an opaque gum-like skin called nyf. 52. 53. Impact-type microdiamonds can indicate ancient impact craters. 54. Some diamonds, such as carbonado diamonds found in South America and Africa, were deposited via asteroid impact about 3 billion years ago. 55. Presolar grains in meteorites contain nanodiamonds of extraterrestrial origin, likely formed in supernovas. 56. Some white dwarf stars are believed to have carbon cores, with the largest known diamond in the universe located 50 light-years away in the constellation Centaurus. 57. Diamond-bearing rock is brought close to the surface through deep-origin volcanic eruptions, forming volcanic pipes. 58. These pipes contain material transported by volcanic action but not ejected before the activity ceased. 59. Diamond-bearing volcanic pipes are closely related to the oldest, coolest regions of continental crust (cratons). 60. Not all pipes contain diamonds, and even fewer are economically viable for mining. 61. The magma in volcanic pipes acts as an elevator, carrying deep-formed rocks, minerals, and fluids upward. 62. Kimberlite deposits are known as blue ground for their deeper serpentinized parts or yellow ground for their near-surface weathered portions. 63. Once diamonds are transported to the surface, they may erode out and be distributed over a large area. 64. A volcanic pipe containing diamonds is known as a primary source, while secondary sources include areas where diamonds accumulate due to erosion. 65. Diamonds have also been found in glacial deposits, though these are not commercially viable sources. 66. Diamonds were first recognized and mined in India, where significant alluvial deposits were found along rivers like the Penner, Krishna, and Godavari. 67. India led the world in diamond production until the mid-18th century when Brazil became the leading source. 68. Diamond production from primary deposits began in the 1870s after the discovery of diamond fields in South Africa. 69. Today, most commercially viable diamond deposits are in Russia, Botswana, Australia, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. 70. In 2005, Russia produced nearly one-fifth of the global diamond output. 71. The diamond industry is broadly divided into gem-grade and industrial-grade categories, with the latter valued for hardness and heat conductivity. 72. Industrial diamonds are used in cutting, drilling, grinding, and polishing applications. 73. Synthetic diamonds have found industrial applications since their invention in the 1950s. 74. Advances in synthetic diamond production are enabling new applications, such as use in semiconductors and heat sinks in electronics. 75. The diamond supply chain is controlled by a few powerful businesses and concentrated in a small number of locations worldwide. 76. The Kimberley Process was introduced to prevent the trading of conflict diamonds used to fund wars and inhumane acts.
